This guide shows how to set up your own component instead of the tutorial pad.
It assumes you have finished the
[capacitance tutorial](../tutorials/capacitance/prepare.qmd).

## Build a GeometryPlan for your component

A `GeometryPlan` connects your component to SCGSim. You give it the component,
its layer stack and its material records; then you assign shapes to conductors.

```python
from scgsim.geometry import GeometryPlan

plan = GeometryPlan(
    component=component,
    root_id="chip",
    layer_stack=layer_stack,
    material_records=material_records,
    coupon_padding_um=coupon_padding_um,
)
```

`component`, `layer_stack` and `material_records` come from your PDK.
`root_id` is the name SCGSim gives the top-level component; every shape ID
starts with it.

### Register placed sub-components

If your component places other components as references, register each
reference you want to keep as a named part:

```python
plan.register_instance("chip/qubit", qubit_ref)
```

Use the actual GDSFactory reference objects. Do not guess paths from flattened
polygon names. Register a parent before its children: `chip/qubit` before
`chip/qubit/junction`. Shapes drawn directly in the top-level component are already
under `chip`.

### List the shapes

Each named shape is an **Entity**. Print their IDs:

```python
print(tuple(entity.semantic_id for entity in plan.entities))
```

### Assign shapes to Nets

A **Net** is one electrical conductor. It can contain several Entities, for
example all the ground-plane pieces. Map each Net name to its Entity IDs:

```python
plan.set_nets({
    "qubit": ("chip/qubit/PAD",),
    "ground": ("chip/GROUND", "chip/qubit/GROUND"),
})
```

Choose the Nets from the circuit you want to model. Shapes in the same Net are
at the same voltage. The [geometry reference](../geometry-sgb.qmd#component-to-backend-geometry-contract)
lists the exact rules. The [Xmon model](../tutorial-xmon-input.qmd) is a larger
example with nested references.

### Add vacuum and freeze the plan

```python
plan.set_vacuum_region(padding=(250.0, 250.0, 1000.0))
snapshot = plan.prepare()
```

`padding` is in micrometres. `prepare()` returns a frozen **snapshot**. Solvers
read the snapshot, not the plan. After you change the geometry, stack, Nets or
vacuum, call `prepare()` again. Editing a summary dictionary does not change
the snapshot.

## Add curved boundaries

By default SCGSim uses the polygons in your GDS. For Palace, you can instead
give exact curves: lines, arcs and splines. SCGSim then meshes the true curve
rather than its polygon approximation. AEDT does not support curves; AEDT runs
use the polygons.

There are two ways to provide curves:

- **Curves drawn in the component.** The component stores
  `BoundaryCurveChainSpec` records in
  `component.info["component_semantics"]["boundary_curves"]`. Each record names
  an Entity, one of its boundaries, and the ordered segments that replace it.
  To add curves after assembly, call `plan.set_boundary_curves(...)` with
  full Entity IDs and assembled coordinates.
- **Curves fitted to GDS points.** If you have only polygon vertices, add a
  `GdsBoundaryReconstructionSpec` in
  `component.info["component_semantics"]["boundary_reconstruction"]`, or call
  `plan.set_boundary_reconstruction(...)`. Only the segments you select become
  curves; the rest stay straight.

SCGSim never smooths polygons on its own.

::: {.callout-note title="Drawn curves win over fitted curves"}
`set_boundary_curves([])` does not remove curves drawn in the component, and
fitting a curve onto a boundary that already has a drawn curve is an error. To
fit curves to polygon data instead, build a separate `GeometryBuildInput`
without the drawn curve and pass it to `SemanticGeometryBuilder`. The
[source-curve reference](../geometry-sgb.qmd#source-curves) has the details.
:::

For a complete curved example, see the
[Circular Pad study](palace-eigenmode.qmd#circular-pad-lc-study).

## Change the physical problem

Different questions need different inputs:

| Question | Also needs |
|---|---|
| Capacitance | Which Nets are terminals and which are Ground |
| Resonant modes | Boundary conditions, and any lumped junction inductance |
| Port response | Ports and their reference conductors |
| Per-unit-length line parameters | A 2D cross section |

[Choose the physical problem](../concepts/problems.qmd) explains each one.

Q3D and Q2D take their own inputs. Q3D builds finite-thickness bodies, either
from a snapshot or written directly; see [Q3D](aedt-q3d.qmd). Q2D takes
rectangles that you draw for the cross section; it does not slice your
component. See [Q2D](aedt-q2d.qmd).

## Change solver settings

Mesh size, element order, adaptive refinement, the eigenmode search frequency
and the number of modes are solver settings, separate from the model. Use a
new run directory for each change, and record what you changed next to the
result so you can compare runs later.

The values in the tutorials are starting points, not recommended accuracy
settings for every model.

## What to rerun after a change

| You changed | Do this |
|---|---|
| Geometry, stack, Nets or vacuum | `plan.prepare()` again, then prepare and run a new solve |
| Boundaries, terminals, ports or junction values | Prepare and run a new solve |
| Mesh or solver settings | Prepare and run a new solve |
| Surface-film margins on saved AEDT fields | [Compute EPR from saved fields](aedt-saved-fields.qmd); no new solve |
| Loss tangents on an existing EPR result | [Change loss assumptions offline](offline-epr.qmd); no solver |

Before running, you can check the model with
[Inspect the source model](source-observations.qmd) and
[Inspect the prepared run](solver-observations.qmd).
